**Gugulethu, Cape Town**

Creating public spaces that more people can enjoy isn’t always easy to do in an overcrowded and overlooked township. But in Gugulethu, a township about 15km from Cape Town, a clean-up and redesign of a waste-filled walkway has created a new safe walkway in the community. It’s also become the vital spark for a handful of other successful community projects. It brings together many different partners, all interested in being caretakers of their strip of public space that has become something locals can be proud of.

### **What was the problem?**

Gugulethu, like many townships, faces problems of public dumping, lack of safety and limited space for new development that can lead to functional public spaces. A pedestrian walkway that connects the Dora Tamana Road and Lolo Mkonto Road had become unusable because of dumping, neglect and criminal elements. It meant people, including local schoolchildren, had to walk further to get to their destinations and the strip of land was left to fall into neglect. It was an eyesore and a critical access route within the township was being lost.

### **How did they fix it?**

In April 2021 community members decided to clean the walkway. Over the next six months a partnership with many different interested parties was formed. It focussed on co-designing, using low-tech and recyclable materials and incorporating as many of the community’s ideas and visions for the space. It would come together as the iThemba Walkway.

The project had many partners. They included the University of Cape Town’s School of Urban Design; local non-profit organisations including ones focused on social justice and food gardening; the Nobantu Primary School; community action groups; street committees and the ward councillor. They met several times to understand needs, priorities and how the community would take ownership of the project.

Kathryn Ewing, a researcher at the University of Cape Town, quoted in [_GroundUp_](https://groundup.org.za/article/community-transforms-crime-hotspot-to-colourful-walkway-for-learners-in-gugulethu/) __said: “We ran three workshops on challenges and opportunities around making the walkway an inclusive and safe space. It was very emotional because it brought up a lot of memories for community members. We also did a climate change workshop with the children and painted our first mural on the walls.”

The focus has been on using low-tech and recycled materials and to bring greening to this small communal space as part of making the upgrading strategy sustainable and cost effective.

Linda Kabedi, a street committee chairperson, said to _GroundUp_: “From the first day the walkway was cleaned, it was not littered or damaged again because of the community’s commitment. It is our responsibility to keep iThemba Way clean and safe.”

On the cards are plans to expand the walkway project to other parts of the township. For iThemba Way there are plans for more murals, a memory wall and co-creating benches and setting up an outdoor movie wall.

### **What makes it work?**

*   **Creating strong partnerships -** Leaning on researchers from the city’s university gave the community more access to resources to take a cleaned-up space to the next level of being more multi-functional and sustainable.
*   **Getting local input -** Various dialogue meetings were held, meaning there was more buy-in, and a greater sense of community ownership for the project.
*   **Using resources wisely -** The emphasis on low-tech interventions and the use of recycled and natural materials kept costs down. It also makes maintenance more affordable and is something community members can do themselves as things need repairing.
*   **Holding the community’s interest -** By incorporating heritage and memory projects, the walkway project helps preserve and enhance the cultural history of the township.
*   **Addressing wider community needs –**Projects like urban farming projects allow residents to grow their own food. It promotes healthy eating and the importance of greening surroundings.
*   **Creating opportunities:** -From the walkway project other initiatives have been sparked. These include a micro-financing and small loans project for small start-ups linked to a skills training programme aimed at building self-sufficiency and resilience.

# Gugulethu becomes the first township to unveil its own logo and anthem

![Image 6: The logo was designed in an open competition among learners from the area’s high schools. Para-Commonwealth gold medallist Ndodomzi Ntutu unveils the logo. Picture: Supplied](https://iol-prod.appspot.com/image/acbee7499e95a8fd4947349995f5311d6b1cbe7f=w700)
The logo was designed in an open competition among learners from the area’s high schools. Para-Commonwealth gold medallist Ndodomzi Ntutu unveils the logo. Picture: Supplied

Cape Town - Gugulethu has become the first township in the country to have an official logo, which was unveiled on Thursday complete with its own anthem.

Proclaimed as a historical moment for the future of the 64-year-old township, the concept is the brainchild of Dr Mzwandile Plaatjie, a psychologist, former principal in Gugulethu and renowned author of five books, including Gugulethu: The Fragments of Unwritten History.

The logo was designed in an open competition among learners from the area’s high schools. The selected entry was the artwork of Ayanda Makhalima, an upcoming designer.

The emblem features the landmark Table Mountain in an orange background, complete with the slogan Siyazingca, “We are Proud”, which is intended to develop a sense of community and pride in the Gugulethu community.

Plaatjie said the concept was triggered by the observation of the emergence of new forms of struggle that posed a threat to the existence of the community. He said the project was inspired by the thought of instilling the idea of tomorrow into the minds of people who were battling to see and care about tomorrow.

Plaatjie said communities would only be transformed by changing the postures of their mind and planting new moral values.

“It came to our minds that we cannot begin to think of solutions without first understanding who we are and identifying ourselves in the context of surrounding challenges facing us as marginalised communities.

“We strongly believe that before we talk, we must identify ourselves and identify the things that (keep) us from developing as a unified community,” he said.

Plaatjie said the noble thing was to create a solid foundation for the next generation to have a strong sense of direction.

“The project has managed to join together the dissipated assemblies of hope that are necessary for creating security for the future of our generation,” he said.

Gugulethu Development Forum chairperson Vincent Domingo said the logo and the anthem would help the community return to its pride and former glory. He said it was now up to the community to take the project forward and he called on local organisations and clubs to adopt the logo and anthem.

Mayor Geordin Hill-Lewis, who expressed his endorsement of the idea, said he was looking forward to seeing the results. Hill-Lewis also encouraged Capetonians to be inspired by the project, irrespective of circumstances.

# Gugulethu becomes the first township to unveil its own logo and anthem

[Mthuthuzeli Ntseku](https://iol.co.za/authors/mthuthuzeli-ntseku/)|Published 3 years ago

Ask AI

2 min

[![Image 4: Add IOL as a preferred source on Google](https://iol.co.za/_next/static/media/iol-google-prefered-black.1cf25725.webp)](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=https%3A%2F%2Fiol.co.za)

[![Image 5: Follow IOL on Google News](https://iol.co.za/_next/static/media/iol-google-news-follow.6c774fa8.webp)](https://news.google.com/publications/CAAqIggKIhxDQklTRHdnTWFnc0tDV2x2YkM1amJ5NTZZU2dBUAE?ceid=ZA:en&oc=3%22)

![Image 6: The logo was designed in an open competition among learners from the area’s high schools. Para-Commonwealth gold medallist Ndodomzi Ntutu unveils the logo. Picture: Supplied](https://iol-prod.appspot.com/image/acbee7499e95a8fd4947349995f5311d6b1cbe7f=w700)
The logo was designed in an open competition among learners from the area’s high schools. Para-Commonwealth gold medallist Ndodomzi Ntutu unveils the logo. Picture: Supplied

Cape Town - Gugulethu has become the first township in the country to have an official logo, which was unveiled on Thursday complete with its own anthem.

Proclaimed as a historical moment for the future of the 64-year-old township, the concept is the brainchild of Dr Mzwandile Plaatjie, a psychologist, former principal in Gugulethu and renowned author of five books, including Gugulethu: The Fragments of Unwritten History.

The logo was designed in an open competition among learners from the area’s high schools. The selected entry was the artwork of Ayanda Makhalima, an upcoming designer.

The emblem features the landmark Table Mountain in an orange background, complete with the slogan Siyazingca, “We are Proud”, which is intended to develop a sense of community and pride in the Gugulethu community.

Plaatjie said the concept was triggered by the observation of the emergence of new forms of struggle that posed a threat to the existence of the community. He said the project was inspired by the thought of instilling the idea of tomorrow into the minds of people who were battling to see and care about tomorrow.

Plaatjie said communities would only be transformed by changing the postures of their mind and planting new moral values.

“It came to our minds that we cannot begin to think of solutions without first understanding who we are and identifying ourselves in the context of surrounding challenges facing us as marginalised communities.

“We strongly believe that before we talk, we must identify ourselves and identify the things that (keep) us from developing as a unified community,” he said.

Plaatjie said the noble thing was to create a solid foundation for the next generation to have a strong sense of direction.

“The project has managed to join together the dissipated assemblies of hope that are necessary for creating security for the future of our generation,” he said.

Gugulethu Development Forum chairperson Vincent Domingo said the logo and the anthem would help the community return to its pride and former glory. He said it was now up to the community to take the project forward and he called on local organisations and clubs to adopt the logo and anthem.

Mayor Geordin Hill-Lewis, who expressed his endorsement of the idea, said he was looking forward to seeing the results. Hill-Lewis also encouraged Capetonians to be inspired by the project, irrespective of circumstances.

## Abstract

Some people with HIV (PWH) test positive multiple times without initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART). We surveyed 496 ART-eligible PWH following routine HIV testing at three clinics in Soweto and Gugulethu, South Africa in 2014–2015. Among repeat positive testers (RPTs) in this cohort, we compared rates of treatment initiation by prior treatment eligibility and assessed psychosocial predictors of treatment initiation in logistic regression models. RPTs represented 33.8% of PWH in this cohort. Less than half of those who reported eligibility for ART on prior testing started treatment upon retesting, in contrast to two thirds of RPTs who were previously ineligible for treatment who started treatment once they learned of their eligibility. Those who reported coping through substance use were more likely to decline treatment versus those not using substances. PWH who test repeatedly represent a vulnerable population at risk for ART non-initiation who may benefit from interventions addressing individualized coping strategies.

**Keywords:**Repeat Positive Testing, Retesting, South Africa, Antiretroviral Treatment Initiation, Coping

## INTRODUCTION

There remains a gap between the 92% of people with HIV (PWH) who know their status and the 75% of those who initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) in South Africa (1), highlighting a need to identify and support persons not engaging in care. Repeat positive testers (RPTs), defined as PWH who continue to test for HIV despite knowing their HIV positive status, have been shown to have a median time of over 12 months from initial diagnosis to enrollment in care, as compared to a median of one month for first-time positive testers (2).

The few studies on repeat positive testing in sub-Saharan Africa have found variation in the proportions of RPTs, as well as their demographic and clinical correlates, depending on the location and method of assessment of repeat positive testing (2–5). A recent retrospective study at a clinic in Cape Town, South Africa found that 308 PWH (25.3% of all PWH in the study) retested despite self-reporting their prior positive diagnosis, which was more common among younger adults ages 15 to 24 years (4). In the same study, an additional 315 PWH, representing 34.7% of all individuals believed to be newly diagnosed, were later found in clinic records to have been diagnosed previously despite non-disclosure to clinic staff, and over half of these individuals had no evidence of prior ART. A clinic and home-based HIV testing campaign in Mozambique found that 36.4% of persons with a positive diagnosis did not disclose their prior result to study staff, which was found to be more common among younger testers ages 18 to 24 years and those with no prior history of ART (3). In Ethiopia, 13.2% of PWH on treatment reported retesting after their first positive result, and this was more common among those testing for a reason other than having symptoms (2). In Kenya, 26.0% of PWH presenting for routine HIV testing in clinics reported in a study survey that they had tested positive previously (5). In this study, those who previously tested positive were more likely to have initiated testing themselves (versus provider-initiated testing) and be ≥40 years old.

Despite evidence of sizable proportions of RPTs among all people testing for HIV, previous studies have not identified which RPTs start treatment after retesting. In particular, despite extensive research on pre-ART loss in South Africa (6–9), it is unknown whether RPTs who already know that they are ART-eligible are less likely to start treatment as compared to those who learn of their ART eligibility upon retesting. Prior to implementation of the “universal test and treat” (UTT) strategy in South Africa in 2016, treatment eligibility guidelines were based in part on CD4 count (10,11). Even in the current UTT era, the history of these CD4 count-based guidelines may still cause confusion regarding treatment eligibility (4) and impact treatment uptake.

In addition, research suggests that RPTs continue to test because they doubt or don’t understand their diagnosis, seek to initiate ART at another facility than where they first tested, or have had a long delay in linkage to care (2,4,5). It has been hypothesized that stigma may also play a role in non-disclosure of a prior positive status when testing (3). However, no studies have examined psychosocial and structural factors associated with starting treatment after retesting among RPTs.

In order to address these gaps in the research, we first estimated the prevalence of repeat positive testing in a South African cohort and characterized socio-demographic and clinical characteristics of RPTs. We then sought to understand which factors were associated with treatment uptake among the RPTs in this cohort. Given that PWH with a lower CD4 count often have more HIV-related symptoms, we hypothesized that RPTs with a lower CD4 count would be more likely to accept treatment upon retesting as compared to RPTs with a higher CD4 count. We also hypothesized that RPTs who were previously ineligible for treatment would be more likely to start treatment upon learning of their new eligibility after retesting as compared to RPTs who retested despite already knowing they were treatment eligible. Finally, we examined a broad set of psychosocial and structural factors which we hypothesized would be associated with treatment uptake among RPTs. Together, these findings may be instructive in identifying RPTs at risk for declining treatment and preemptively addressing barriers for these patients so as to convert repeat testing engagement into treatment initiation.

### Theoretical Framework

To inform our selection of psychosocial and structural measures, we drew on the Theory of Triadic Influence (TTI), which has been applied to understanding barriers to ART initiation in South Africa (12) and can be used to better understand reasons for ART initiation or non-initiation among RPTs. TTI posits that there are three independent and integrated streams of influence on health behaviors: individual-level factors, social-level factors, and structural-level factors (13). Individual-level factors shown to support treatment initiation for PWH include positive coping skills (14,15), greater knowledge of HIV (16), and higher perceived ART efficacy (17), whereas feeling healthy (18) and depressive symptoms (19) have been shown to impede ART uptake. Social-level factors for PWH include social support, which can help facilitate treatment initiation (20,21). Conversely, the fear of social isolation stemming from unintended disclosure and perceived stigma can be a deterrent to taking ART (18). Structural level factors hindering PWH’s uptake of treatment may include clinic-related barriers, such as distance to clinic, lack of public transportation, long clinic queues, and treatment stock-outs (22).

## METHODS

### Participants, Study Setting and Procedures

Details of the study are described previously (23). We used data from a prospective cohort of 500 ART-eligible PWH recruited from July 2014 to July 2015 following routine Voluntary Testing and Counseling (VCT) for HIV at one of three healthcare facilities in Soweto and Gugulethu. Soweto is the largest urban township in South Africa with an estimated 1.7 million people and adjoins Johannesburg within Gauteng Province, which has an adult HIV prevalence of almost 18% (24,25). Gugulethu, located by Cape Town in the Western Cape, is a smaller urban township with approximately 100,000 people (26). Of all the South African provinces, the Western Cape has the lowest adult HIV prevalence at close to 13% (25).

Individuals who tested positive had blood drawn for a CD4 count, and PWH were recruited and enrolled as they received their CD4 counts one week later. Pregnant women and children were excluded because they qualified for intensive adherence support under South African guidelines. All participants were referred to clinic counselors or social workers to discuss ART initiation. Demographics and HIV test results, including CD4 count, were recorded in a clinical directory.

### Treatment Eligibility

Treatment eligibility was determined by South African guidelines, which changed during the study period. Before January 1, 2015, PWH were eligible for treatment who had a CD4 count ≤350 cells/μL, an advanced clinical diagnosis including WHO Stage III/IV HIV illness, or who had a CD4 count between 350 and 500 cells/μL and were “ready and motivated to start” (11). After January 1, 2015, the CD4 count threshold changed to ≤500 cells/μL with the same clinical criteria. While all participants were eligible for ART upon study enrollment as part of study eligibility criteria, only some RPTs were previously ART-eligible at the time of their prior positive testing.

### Data Collection and Measures

Participants were surveyed by trained multi-lingual interviewers to assess demographics (gender, age, marital status, children, employment status), self-reported prior testing status, primary reason for testing (symptoms, insurance, partner died, pregnancy, employment, general check-up, CD4 check), and psychosocial factors. Tobacco and alcohol use were not asked in the study survey but rather in the VCT visit prior to study enrollment. The psychosocial factors, described previously (23), were selected on the basis of prior qualitative work (18) and the TTI. Individual-level factors included HIV knowledge (modified HIV-Knowledge Questionnaire-18 scale) (27), perceived ART efficacy (Perceived Antiretroviral Treatment scale) (28), AIDS symptoms (Istituto Superiore di Sanita-HIV Symptoms scale) (29), coping strategies (Brief Cope scale, including self-distraction, denial, substance use, disengagement, venting and self-blame) (30), religious coping (Brief RCOPE scale) (31), quality of life (modified from AIDS Clinical Trial Groups SF-21 Measure) (32), depression (PHQ-9 scale) (33), perceived stress (modified Perceived Stress scale) (34), and fatalism (modified Meyer-Weitz Fatalism scale) (35). Social level factors were evaluated by measuring perceived social support (Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support scale) (36). Structural level factors were evaluated by measuring structural barriers to clinic (modified Barriers to HIV Medical Care scale) (37). These scales were translated into Zulu for participants in Soweto and into Xhosa for participants in Gugulethu.

ART initiation at six months was determined by accessing routine laboratory data in South Africa’s National Health Laboratory Service (NHLS). Initiation at six months post-test was selected in the parent study given that there can be a significant lag between diagnosis to ART initiation, and multiple other studies measure ART initiation within 6 months (38,39). Participants were considered to have initiated ART based on the date of a test of kidney function (creatinine clearance) reported to NHLS. Creatine clearance is routinely performed prior to initiating Tenofovir, a standard, first-line regimen in South Africa. NHLS provides laboratory services to all public-sector facilities in the country, and this method of recording ART initiation in NHLS has been validated as an accurate way to impute treatment initiation for PWH receiving public sector healthcare in South Africa (40).

### Statistical Analysis

We estimated the prevalence of RPTs in our cohort by calculating the proportion of self-reported RPTs among all participants who reported on prior testing status. We compared socio-demographic characteristics, reason for testing, CD4 count, and ART initiation within six months of testing between first-time positive testers and RPTs using Chi-square tests, or Fisher’s exact tests when cell counts were ≤5. Among RPTs, we compared CD4 count ≤350 cells/μL, prior ART eligibility, and primary testing reason (among RPTs previously eligible for treatment) between those who initiated ART within six months of testing and those who did not, again using Chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests where cell counts were ≤5. We used Student’s t-tests to compare psychosocial and structural measures between RPTs who did and did not initiate ART, with the exception of measures for which we observed high skewness, where we used Wilcoxon rank sum tests instead. In addition, with each psychosocial measure as a predictor, we used logistic regression to model our outcome of treatment initiation at six months, controlling for age, sex, CD4 count >350 cells/μL, married, site, and CD4 count check as the reason for testing. We chose to control for these factors given they may influence psychosocial measures as well as treatment initiation (38,41,42), but they are not along the causal pathway from each psychosocial measure to starting treatment.

### Ethics

The Human Subjects Committees at Partners Healthcare, the University of Witwatersrand Ethics Committee, the Gauteng Department of Health, and the University of Cape Town Human Research Ethics Committee approved the study. All participants provided written informed consent. Study data were collected and managed using Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap), a secure, web-based tool hosted at Partners Healthcare (43).

## RESULTS

### Socio-demographic and Clinical Characteristics of Repeat Positive Testers

Over the study period of one year, a total of 1,071 adults presented for testing and were found to be positive for HIV and eligible for ART. Of these, 711 returned for their CD4 count results within six weeks and 667 were approached for inclusion in the study. Of the 500 participants in the original cohort, 496 provided survey data regarding whether they had previously tested positive for HIV and thus were included in these analyses. RPTs represented 169/496 (34.1%) of total testers (Table I and Figure 1). A higher proportion of women were RPTs (37.6%) than men (28.1%) (χ 2=4.673, p=0.031), and Soweto had a greater proportion of RPTs than Gugulethu (42.9% vs. 28.2%, χ 2=11.508, p=0.001). A greater proportion of participants with a CD4 count ≤350 cells/μL were first-time positive testers in comparison to RPTs (68.8% vs. 31.2%, χ 2=5.647, p=0.017). RPTs and first-time positive testers did not differ in terms of age, marital status, number of children, employment status or substance use.

Symptom development, general check-up, and checking CD4 count were the three most common reasons for all participants to present for testing. CD4 count check was the most common reason (40.2%) for testing among RPTs, and among all participants who reported this reason for testing, the majority were RPTs (94.4%, Fisher’s exact test, p<0.001). The second most common reason for testing among RPTs was the development of symptoms (37.3%). For first-time positive testers, symptom development was the most common reason for testing (69.7%), and first-time positive testers represented a greater proportion of all participants who presented for symptoms (78.4%, Fisher’s exact test, p<0.001).

### CD4 Count, Prior Eligibility, and Treatment Initiation Among Repeat Positive Testers

ART initiation at six months after testing was similar between RPTs and first-time positive testers (60.9% vs. 61.5%, χ 2=0.013, p=0.910). Among RPTs only, ART initiation was also similar between RPTs with CD4 count ≤350 cells/μL and CD4 count >350 cells/μL (Table II). RPTs were composed of 16.4% PWH previously eligible for treatment on the basis of their CD4 count and 83.6% PWH newly eligible for treatment (Figure 1). Examining RPTs by prior treatment eligibility revealed that among RPTs who were newly eligible for ART, only 36.2% declined it, whereas among RPTs previously eligible for treatment, 56.0% continued to decline treatment (χ 2=3.654, p=0.161). Within the subset of RPTs previously eligible for treatment, we found no difference in ART initiation comparing those who did and did not present for symptoms and comparing those who did and did not present to check their CD4 count.

### Psychosocial and Structural Correlates and Predictors of Treatment Initiation Among Repeat Positive Testers

Among all RPTs, two individual-level coping strategies (measured within the Brief Cope scale (30)) were associated with declining treatment as compared to treatment initiation in our unadjusted analyses: self-distraction (on a scale of 2 [least] to 8 [most]: mean 5.03 vs. mean 4.37, t=2.009, p=0.046) and substance use (on a scale of 2 [least] to 8 [most]: mean 3.23 vs. mean 2.54, z=2.347, p=0.007) (Table III). Other factors, including factors at the individual level as well as factors at the social and structural levels, were not found to have a significant association with treatment non-initiation among RPTs. In adjusted logistic regression models in which each psychosocial and structural measure was controlled for the sociodemographic and clinical variables indicated previously (Table IV), only coping through substance use predicted declining treatment among RPTs (aOR=0.79, 95% CI 0.65–0.97, p=0.025, z=−2.24). Other psychosocial and structural factors were not found to significantly predict treatment initiation among RPTs.

## DISCUSSION

In this study, we found that over one third of our participants who presented for testing self-identified as repeat testers. This finding builds on prior literature in both the pre-UTT (2,3) and post-UTT (4) eras showing that a substantial proportion of people who are found to have HIV are repeat positive testers. This suggests that the numbers of people newly diagnosed in testing campaigns may be lower than believed (3). Unlike prior research showing that repeat testing is more common in young adults <24 years (3,4) and older adults >40 years (5), we did not find differences comparing RPTs to first-time positive testers by age. However, our overall proportions of testers in these age groups were low (9.9% 18–24 years and 28.1% >40 years), which may have masked our ability to detect significant differences among these age groups.

The most common reason RPTs tested was to determine their CD4 count (40.2%). In the era of CD4 count-based treatment guidelines in South Africa, measurements of CD4 counts were given on initial testing, and then given annually for persons not on treatment to determine ART eligibility (44). HIV testing was not a prerequisite to CD4 count testing if a PWH was already known to a clinic; thus, it is possible that RPTs who reported HIV testing in order to check their CD4 count were seeking care at a new clinic, which research has shown may be due in part to feelings of shame and a desire to reinvent oneself as a new HIV patient (45). Prior research on RPTs also suggests that RPTs are more likely to retest at a different facility from where they were initially diagnosed (2). In this cohort of RPTs, those who reported testing for HIV in order to check their CD4 count may have wanted to monitor their disease progression without having to wait for their annual check.

In addition, nearly as many RPTs reported testing due to the development of symptoms (37.3%) as tested to check their CD4 count. Together, these findings extend prior research showing that progression in the HIV care continuum is not always linear; rather, some PWH cycle in and out of care through “side doors,” precipited by symptoms or a motivating event (46,47). This fluidity highlights both the on-the-ground complexities of care engagement as well as the need to promote linkage to treatment for those PWH who already know their serostatus, particularly before they become ill.

Our findings also add to prior literature by showing that RPTs are not only at risk for not being on treatment at the time of retesting (3,4), but also at risk for not starting treatment within six months after retesting. We found no difference in rates of of treatment initiation between RPTs with CD4 count ≤350 cells/μL as compared to RPTs CD4 count >350 cells/μL, despite our hypothesis that RPTs with a lower CD4 count would have more HIV-related symptoms and thus be more likely to start treatment. Literature has shown that PWH may experience a subjective feeling of health and wellness despite their actual clinical status, which may explain why having a low CD4 count alone does not predict treatment uptake (18). We also hypothesized that more RPTs who were previously ineligible for treatment would start it upon newly learning of their eligibility as compared to RPTs who were previously eligible for treatment and continued to retest regardless. We did not find a statistically significant difference to support this hypothesis. However, this may be due to a lack of power given our small sample size of only 25 RPTs previously eligible for treatment. Despite this, we observed that almost two thirds of RPTs who were previously ineligible for treatment did start it once they learned of their eligibility, in contrast to less than half of RPTs who were previously eligible for treatment and started it upon retesting. CD4 count-based guidelines do not explain why over half of the RPTs who were previously eligible for treatment continued to decline it, despite their willingness to retest and the fact that treatment was available in the public sector at no cost (48).

Research on PWH in South Africa has shown that feeling healthy, fear of stigmatization, and poor quality pre- and post-test counseling are important factors related to ART delay and refusal (14,49), though it is less well understood how these PWH subsequently interact with HIV services, if at all. Our study suggests that not all those who decline treatment fully disengage with HIV services; rather, repeat testing may be one way that PWH who are not on treatment strategically manage their disease in lieu of or prior to ultimately starting treatment. For example, they may test for HIV to see if they are still HIV positive, to check whether their disease has progressed (as measured by CD4 count testing), and to find out what counseling they will receive before and after testing. Unlike PWH not on treatment who remain in the community, RPTs present an important opportunity for clinic staff to conduct an intervention to help them to start treatment.

It is critical, therefore, to understand which “tipping points” motivate treatment initiation among RPTs or conversely which factors are associated with continuing to decline it. Comparing previously ART-eligible RPTs who started treatment to those who did not start, we found no differences in reasons for testing. However, an individual-level factor related to coping predicted declining treatment among all RPTs. Coping, the process by which individuals manage their responses to stressors (50,51), has been shown to be important in influencing treatment initiation for PWH (15,52). Adaptive coping, which involves strategies to respond to stressors in healthy ways (e.g. problem-solving) (53), may facilitate acceptance of an HIV diagnosis and mitigate the perceived risk of starting treatment among adults presenting for HIV testing in Soweto (18). Conversely, maladaptive coping, such as denial (53), is associated with non-initiation of ART for PWH in South Africa (15).

In our cohort of RPTs, coping through substance use, a maladaptive strategy, predicted treatment refusal. Historically, alcohol, tobacco, and cannibis have been the most commonly used substances in South Africa (54), although growing numbers of people inject heroin (55) and use non-injection drugs, such as methamphetamine and crack cocaine (56). Research has shown that substance use is associated with a range of poor outcomes for PWH (57,58), attributed to complex factors including substances’ effects on PWH’s cognitive ability, which impact their ability to engage in care, as well as concerns about ART and alcohol interactions leading PWH to skip ART when drinking (59). Additionally, substance use may reflect other underlying maladaptive coping strategies (60,61), inaccess to mental health care (62), and other life stresors (63), including sexual violence and unemployment, which collectively make it hard for PWH to stay engaged in HIV care. Therefore, substance use screening at the time of repeat HIV testing may help to predict those at risk for not starting treatment and allow for targeted intervention strategies to counsel on substance use as well as on adaptive coping behaviors to support treatment initiation among RPTs. Studies have shown that individualized and group delivery methods of cognitive behavioral interventions and stress management approaches can be effective across heterogeneous groups of PWH (64–67). Particularly given the heavy counseling burden on HIV lay counselors and providers of HIV testing in South Africa (68), it is important to identify RPTs as PWH who may particularly benefit from targeted counseling and tailor approaches to their needs.

### Limitations and Future Directions

We found no difference in ART initiation between RPTs and first-time positive testers; however, differences may have been masked by the presence of future RPTs among first-time testers. We also found no association between treatment initiation and the other psychosocial factors we assessed, although perceived ART inefficacy (69), symptoms (70), fatalism (71), and clinic barriers (72) have been shown previously to be associated with treatment refusal. Given that these findings did not emerge in this study, we suggest further research to replicate and further explore them. In addition, data on prior testing was by self-report, which is subject to recall bias and may also underestimate the true proportion of RPTs, as it has been shown that around one third of persons thought to be newly diagnosed do not disclose their positive status when testing (3,4). Non-disclosure of a positive status to study staff has also been a concern in recent studies evaluating HIV self-testing among men (73–75). As discussed, this cohort was recruited in the era of CD4 count-based guidelines for treatment eligibility, limiting our ability to generalize these findings in today’s UTT era. However, recent research finding repeat positive testing in South Africa (4,75) suggests that this phenomenon is not limited to the pre-UTT era. A further limitation is that the sample from the main study was limited to people who returned for their CD4 count within six weeks, potentially biasing our results towards individuals relatively more likely to be engaged in the health system than those who did not return for their CD4 count within that time frame. Lastly, our sample sizes of total RPTs and previously ART-eligible RPTs are relatively small, limiting our ability to detect statistically significant differences in these analyses, including the non-significant findings for the other psychosocial factors examined. Qualitative research may help to further elucidate the psychosocial and structural drivers of repeat testing among PWH and the factors influencing their treatment initiation.

## CONCLUSIONS

The prevalence of repeat testing among PWH suggests that testing may overestimate the proportion of newly diagnosed individuals, highlighting the complexity of ways in which PWH engage in HIV care as well as the importance of linkage in order to reach 95–95-95 goals. RPTs may be retesting as a way of managing their diagnosis instead of or prior to starting treatment. In fact, a significant cohort of PWH do not start treatment despite repeat testing, especially those previously eligible for treatment and those using substances. RPT’s engagement in care by virtue of repeat testing offers opportunities to identify these vulnerable PWH and to tailor counseling interventions to address their individualized coping mechanisms and promote treatment initiation.

## Abstract

Some people with HIV (PWH) test positive multiple times without initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART). We surveyed 496 ART-eligible PWH following routine HIV testing at three clinics in Soweto and Gugulethu, South Africa in 2014–2015. Among repeat positive testers (RPTs) in this cohort, we compared rates of treatment initiation by prior treatment eligibility and assessed psychosocial predictors of treatment initiation in logistic regression models. RPTs represented 33.8% of PWH in this cohort. Less than half of those who reported eligibility for ART on prior testing started treatment upon retesting, in contrast to two thirds of RPTs who were previously ineligible for treatment who started treatment once they learned of their eligibility. Those who reported coping through substance use were more likely to decline treatment versus those not using substances. PWH who test repeatedly represent a vulnerable population at risk for ART non-initiation who may benefit from interventions addressing individualized coping strategies.

**Keywords:**Repeat Positive Testing, Retesting, South Africa, Antiretroviral Treatment Initiation, Coping

## INTRODUCTION

There remains a gap between the 92% of people with HIV (PWH) who know their status and the 75% of those who initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) in South Africa (1), highlighting a need to identify and support persons not engaging in care. Repeat positive testers (RPTs), defined as PWH who continue to test for HIV despite knowing their HIV positive status, have been shown to have a median time of over 12 months from initial diagnosis to enrollment in care, as compared to a median of one month for first-time positive testers (2).

The few studies on repeat positive testing in sub-Saharan Africa have found variation in the proportions of RPTs, as well as their demographic and clinical correlates, depending on the location and method of assessment of repeat positive testing (2–5). A recent retrospective study at a clinic in Cape Town, South Africa found that 308 PWH (25.3% of all PWH in the study) retested despite self-reporting their prior positive diagnosis, which was more common among younger adults ages 15 to 24 years (4). In the same study, an additional 315 PWH, representing 34.7% of all individuals believed to be newly diagnosed, were later found in clinic records to have been diagnosed previously despite non-disclosure to clinic staff, and over half of these individuals had no evidence of prior ART. A clinic and home-based HIV testing campaign in Mozambique found that 36.4% of persons with a positive diagnosis did not disclose their prior result to study staff, which was found to be more common among younger testers ages 18 to 24 years and those with no prior history of ART (3). In Ethiopia, 13.2% of PWH on treatment reported retesting after their first positive result, and this was more common among those testing for a reason other than having symptoms (2). In Kenya, 26.0% of PWH presenting for routine HIV testing in clinics reported in a study survey that they had tested positive previously (5). In this study, those who previously tested positive were more likely to have initiated testing themselves (versus provider-initiated testing) and be ≥40 years old.

Despite evidence of sizable proportions of RPTs among all people testing for HIV, previous studies have not identified which RPTs start treatment after retesting. In particular, despite extensive research on pre-ART loss in South Africa (6–9), it is unknown whether RPTs who already know that they are ART-eligible are less likely to start treatment as compared to those who learn of their ART eligibility upon retesting. Prior to implementation of the “universal test and treat” (UTT) strategy in South Africa in 2016, treatment eligibility guidelines were based in part on CD4 count (10,11). Even in the current UTT era, the history of these CD4 count-based guidelines may still cause confusion regarding treatment eligibility (4) and impact treatment uptake.

In addition, research suggests that RPTs continue to test because they doubt or don’t understand their diagnosis, seek to initiate ART at another facility than where they first tested, or have had a long delay in linkage to care (2,4,5). It has been hypothesized that stigma may also play a role in non-disclosure of a prior positive status when testing (3). However, no studies have examined psychosocial and structural factors associated with starting treatment after retesting among RPTs.

In order to address these gaps in the research, we first estimated the prevalence of repeat positive testing in a South African cohort and characterized socio-demographic and clinical characteristics of RPTs. We then sought to understand which factors were associated with treatment uptake among the RPTs in this cohort. Given that PWH with a lower CD4 count often have more HIV-related symptoms, we hypothesized that RPTs with a lower CD4 count would be more likely to accept treatment upon retesting as compared to RPTs with a higher CD4 count. We also hypothesized that RPTs who were previously ineligible for treatment would be more likely to start treatment upon learning of their new eligibility after retesting as compared to RPTs who retested despite already knowing they were treatment eligible. Finally, we examined a broad set of psychosocial and structural factors which we hypothesized would be associated with treatment uptake among RPTs. Together, these findings may be instructive in identifying RPTs at risk for declining treatment and preemptively addressing barriers for these patients so as to convert repeat testing engagement into treatment initiation.

### Theoretical Framework

To inform our selection of psychosocial and structural measures, we drew on the Theory of Triadic Influence (TTI), which has been applied to understanding barriers to ART initiation in South Africa (12) and can be used to better understand reasons for ART initiation or non-initiation among RPTs. TTI posits that there are three independent and integrated streams of influence on health behaviors: individual-level factors, social-level factors, and structural-level factors (13). Individual-level factors shown to support treatment initiation for PWH include positive coping skills (14,15), greater knowledge of HIV (16), and higher perceived ART efficacy (17), whereas feeling healthy (18) and depressive symptoms (19) have been shown to impede ART uptake. Social-level factors for PWH include social support, which can help facilitate treatment initiation (20,21). Conversely, the fear of social isolation stemming from unintended disclosure and perceived stigma can be a deterrent to taking ART (18). Structural level factors hindering PWH’s uptake of treatment may include clinic-related barriers, such as distance to clinic, lack of public transportation, long clinic queues, and treatment stock-outs (22).

## METHODS

### Participants, Study Setting and Procedures

Details of the study are described previously (23). We used data from a prospective cohort of 500 ART-eligible PWH recruited from July 2014 to July 2015 following routine Voluntary Testing and Counseling (VCT) for HIV at one of three healthcare facilities in Soweto and Gugulethu. Soweto is the largest urban township in South Africa with an estimated 1.7 million people and adjoins Johannesburg within Gauteng Province, which has an adult HIV prevalence of almost 18% (24,25). Gugulethu, located by Cape Town in the Western Cape, is a smaller urban township with approximately 100,000 people (26). Of all the South African provinces, the Western Cape has the lowest adult HIV prevalence at close to 13% (25).

Individuals who tested positive had blood drawn for a CD4 count, and PWH were recruited and enrolled as they received their CD4 counts one week later. Pregnant women and children were excluded because they qualified for intensive adherence support under South African guidelines. All participants were referred to clinic counselors or social workers to discuss ART initiation. Demographics and HIV test results, including CD4 count, were recorded in a clinical directory.

### Treatment Eligibility

Treatment eligibility was determined by South African guidelines, which changed during the study period. Before January 1, 2015, PWH were eligible for treatment who had a CD4 count ≤350 cells/μL, an advanced clinical diagnosis including WHO Stage III/IV HIV illness, or who had a CD4 count between 350 and 500 cells/μL and were “ready and motivated to start” (11). After January 1, 2015, the CD4 count threshold changed to ≤500 cells/μL with the same clinical criteria. While all participants were eligible for ART upon study enrollment as part of study eligibility criteria, only some RPTs were previously ART-eligible at the time of their prior positive testing.

### Data Collection and Measures

Participants were surveyed by trained multi-lingual interviewers to assess demographics (gender, age, marital status, children, employment status), self-reported prior testing status, primary reason for testing (symptoms, insurance, partner died, pregnancy, employment, general check-up, CD4 check), and psychosocial factors. Tobacco and alcohol use were not asked in the study survey but rather in the VCT visit prior to study enrollment. The psychosocial factors, described previously (23), were selected on the basis of prior qualitative work (18) and the TTI. Individual-level factors included HIV knowledge (modified HIV-Knowledge Questionnaire-18 scale) (27), perceived ART efficacy (Perceived Antiretroviral Treatment scale) (28), AIDS symptoms (Istituto Superiore di Sanita-HIV Symptoms scale) (29), coping strategies (Brief Cope scale, including self-distraction, denial, substance use, disengagement, venting and self-blame) (30), religious coping (Brief RCOPE scale) (31), quality of life (modified from AIDS Clinical Trial Groups SF-21 Measure) (32), depression (PHQ-9 scale) (33), perceived stress (modified Perceived Stress scale) (34), and fatalism (modified Meyer-Weitz Fatalism scale) (35). Social level factors were evaluated by measuring perceived social support (Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support scale) (36). Structural level factors were evaluated by measuring structural barriers to clinic (modified Barriers to HIV Medical Care scale) (37). These scales were translated into Zulu for participants in Soweto and into Xhosa for participants in Gugulethu.

ART initiation at six months was determined by accessing routine laboratory data in South Africa’s National Health Laboratory Service (NHLS). Initiation at six months post-test was selected in the parent study given that there can be a significant lag between diagnosis to ART initiation, and multiple other studies measure ART initiation within 6 months (38,39). Participants were considered to have initiated ART based on the date of a test of kidney function (creatinine clearance) reported to NHLS. Creatine clearance is routinely performed prior to initiating Tenofovir, a standard, first-line regimen in South Africa. NHLS provides laboratory services to all public-sector facilities in the country, and this method of recording ART initiation in NHLS has been validated as an accurate way to impute treatment initiation for PWH receiving public sector healthcare in South Africa (40).

### Statistical Analysis

We estimated the prevalence of RPTs in our cohort by calculating the proportion of self-reported RPTs among all participants who reported on prior testing status. We compared socio-demographic characteristics, reason for testing, CD4 count, and ART initiation within six months of testing between first-time positive testers and RPTs using Chi-square tests, or Fisher’s exact tests when cell counts were ≤5. Among RPTs, we compared CD4 count ≤350 cells/μL, prior ART eligibility, and primary testing reason (among RPTs previously eligible for treatment) between those who initiated ART within six months of testing and those who did not, again using Chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests where cell counts were ≤5. We used Student’s t-tests to compare psychosocial and structural measures between RPTs who did and did not initiate ART, with the exception of measures for which we observed high skewness, where we used Wilcoxon rank sum tests instead. In addition, with each psychosocial measure as a predictor, we used logistic regression to model our outcome of treatment initiation at six months, controlling for age, sex, CD4 count >350 cells/μL, married, site, and CD4 count check as the reason for testing. We chose to control for these factors given they may influence psychosocial measures as well as treatment initiation (38,41,42), but they are not along the causal pathway from each psychosocial measure to starting treatment.

### Ethics

The Human Subjects Committees at Partners Healthcare, the University of Witwatersrand Ethics Committee, the Gauteng Department of Health, and the University of Cape Town Human Research Ethics Committee approved the study. All participants provided written informed consent. Study data were collected and managed using Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap), a secure, web-based tool hosted at Partners Healthcare (43).

## RESULTS

### Socio-demographic and Clinical Characteristics of Repeat Positive Testers

Over the study period of one year, a total of 1,071 adults presented for testing and were found to be positive for HIV and eligible for ART. Of these, 711 returned for their CD4 count results within six weeks and 667 were approached for inclusion in the study. Of the 500 participants in the original cohort, 496 provided survey data regarding whether they had previously tested positive for HIV and thus were included in these analyses. RPTs represented 169/496 (34.1%) of total testers (Table I and Figure 1). A higher proportion of women were RPTs (37.6%) than men (28.1%) (χ 2=4.673, p=0.031), and Soweto had a greater proportion of RPTs than Gugulethu (42.9% vs. 28.2%, χ 2=11.508, p=0.001). A greater proportion of participants with a CD4 count ≤350 cells/μL were first-time positive testers in comparison to RPTs (68.8% vs. 31.2%, χ 2=5.647, p=0.017). RPTs and first-time positive testers did not differ in terms of age, marital status, number of children, employment status or substance use.

Symptom development, general check-up, and checking CD4 count were the three most common reasons for all participants to present for testing. CD4 count check was the most common reason (40.2%) for testing among RPTs, and among all participants who reported this reason for testing, the majority were RPTs (94.4%, Fisher’s exact test, p<0.001). The second most common reason for testing among RPTs was the development of symptoms (37.3%). For first-time positive testers, symptom development was the most common reason for testing (69.7%), and first-time positive testers represented a greater proportion of all participants who presented for symptoms (78.4%, Fisher’s exact test, p<0.001).

### CD4 Count, Prior Eligibility, and Treatment Initiation Among Repeat Positive Testers

ART initiation at six months after testing was similar between RPTs and first-time positive testers (60.9% vs. 61.5%, χ 2=0.013, p=0.910). Among RPTs only, ART initiation was also similar between RPTs with CD4 count ≤350 cells/μL and CD4 count >350 cells/μL (Table II). RPTs were composed of 16.4% PWH previously eligible for treatment on the basis of their CD4 count and 83.6% PWH newly eligible for treatment (Figure 1). Examining RPTs by prior treatment eligibility revealed that among RPTs who were newly eligible for ART, only 36.2% declined it, whereas among RPTs previously eligible for treatment, 56.0% continued to decline treatment (χ 2=3.654, p=0.161). Within the subset of RPTs previously eligible for treatment, we found no difference in ART initiation comparing those who did and did not present for symptoms and comparing those who did and did not present to check their CD4 count.

### Psychosocial and Structural Correlates and Predictors of Treatment Initiation Among Repeat Positive Testers

Among all RPTs, two individual-level coping strategies (measured within the Brief Cope scale (30)) were associated with declining treatment as compared to treatment initiation in our unadjusted analyses: self-distraction (on a scale of 2 [least] to 8 [most]: mean 5.03 vs. mean 4.37, t=2.009, p=0.046) and substance use (on a scale of 2 [least] to 8 [most]: mean 3.23 vs. mean 2.54, z=2.347, p=0.007) (Table III). Other factors, including factors at the individual level as well as factors at the social and structural levels, were not found to have a significant association with treatment non-initiation among RPTs. In adjusted logistic regression models in which each psychosocial and structural measure was controlled for the sociodemographic and clinical variables indicated previously (Table IV), only coping through substance use predicted declining treatment among RPTs (aOR=0.79, 95% CI 0.65–0.97, p=0.025, z=−2.24). Other psychosocial and structural factors were not found to significantly predict treatment initiation among RPTs.

## DISCUSSION

In this study, we found that over one third of our participants who presented for testing self-identified as repeat testers. This finding builds on prior literature in both the pre-UTT (2,3) and post-UTT (4) eras showing that a substantial proportion of people who are found to have HIV are repeat positive testers. This suggests that the numbers of people newly diagnosed in testing campaigns may be lower than believed (3). Unlike prior research showing that repeat testing is more common in young adults <24 years (3,4) and older adults >40 years (5), we did not find differences comparing RPTs to first-time positive testers by age. However, our overall proportions of testers in these age groups were low (9.9% 18–24 years and 28.1% >40 years), which may have masked our ability to detect significant differences among these age groups.

The most common reason RPTs tested was to determine their CD4 count (40.2%). In the era of CD4 count-based treatment guidelines in South Africa, measurements of CD4 counts were given on initial testing, and then given annually for persons not on treatment to determine ART eligibility (44). HIV testing was not a prerequisite to CD4 count testing if a PWH was already known to a clinic; thus, it is possible that RPTs who reported HIV testing in order to check their CD4 count were seeking care at a new clinic, which research has shown may be due in part to feelings of shame and a desire to reinvent oneself as a new HIV patient (45). Prior research on RPTs also suggests that RPTs are more likely to retest at a different facility from where they were initially diagnosed (2). In this cohort of RPTs, those who reported testing for HIV in order to check their CD4 count may have wanted to monitor their disease progression without having to wait for their annual check.

In addition, nearly as many RPTs reported testing due to the development of symptoms (37.3%) as tested to check their CD4 count. Together, these findings extend prior research showing that progression in the HIV care continuum is not always linear; rather, some PWH cycle in and out of care through “side doors,” precipited by symptoms or a motivating event (46,47). This fluidity highlights both the on-the-ground complexities of care engagement as well as the need to promote linkage to treatment for those PWH who already know their serostatus, particularly before they become ill.

Our findings also add to prior literature by showing that RPTs are not only at risk for not being on treatment at the time of retesting (3,4), but also at risk for not starting treatment within six months after retesting. We found no difference in rates of of treatment initiation between RPTs with CD4 count ≤350 cells/μL as compared to RPTs CD4 count >350 cells/μL, despite our hypothesis that RPTs with a lower CD4 count would have more HIV-related symptoms and thus be more likely to start treatment. Literature has shown that PWH may experience a subjective feeling of health and wellness despite their actual clinical status, which may explain why having a low CD4 count alone does not predict treatment uptake (18). We also hypothesized that more RPTs who were previously ineligible for treatment would start it upon newly learning of their eligibility as compared to RPTs who were previously eligible for treatment and continued to retest regardless. We did not find a statistically significant difference to support this hypothesis. However, this may be due to a lack of power given our small sample size of only 25 RPTs previously eligible for treatment. Despite this, we observed that almost two thirds of RPTs who were previously ineligible for treatment did start it once they learned of their eligibility, in contrast to less than half of RPTs who were previously eligible for treatment and started it upon retesting. CD4 count-based guidelines do not explain why over half of the RPTs who were previously eligible for treatment continued to decline it, despite their willingness to retest and the fact that treatment was available in the public sector at no cost (48).

Research on PWH in South Africa has shown that feeling healthy, fear of stigmatization, and poor quality pre- and post-test counseling are important factors related to ART delay and refusal (14,49), though it is less well understood how these PWH subsequently interact with HIV services, if at all. Our study suggests that not all those who decline treatment fully disengage with HIV services; rather, repeat testing may be one way that PWH who are not on treatment strategically manage their disease in lieu of or prior to ultimately starting treatment. For example, they may test for HIV to see if they are still HIV positive, to check whether their disease has progressed (as measured by CD4 count testing), and to find out what counseling they will receive before and after testing. Unlike PWH not on treatment who remain in the community, RPTs present an important opportunity for clinic staff to conduct an intervention to help them to start treatment.

It is critical, therefore, to understand which “tipping points” motivate treatment initiation among RPTs or conversely which factors are associated with continuing to decline it. Comparing previously ART-eligible RPTs who started treatment to those who did not start, we found no differences in reasons for testing. However, an individual-level factor related to coping predicted declining treatment among all RPTs. Coping, the process by which individuals manage their responses to stressors (50,51), has been shown to be important in influencing treatment initiation for PWH (15,52). Adaptive coping, which involves strategies to respond to stressors in healthy ways (e.g. problem-solving) (53), may facilitate acceptance of an HIV diagnosis and mitigate the perceived risk of starting treatment among adults presenting for HIV testing in Soweto (18). Conversely, maladaptive coping, such as denial (53), is associated with non-initiation of ART for PWH in South Africa (15).

In our cohort of RPTs, coping through substance use, a maladaptive strategy, predicted treatment refusal. Historically, alcohol, tobacco, and cannibis have been the most commonly used substances in South Africa (54), although growing numbers of people inject heroin (55) and use non-injection drugs, such as methamphetamine and crack cocaine (56). Research has shown that substance use is associated with a range of poor outcomes for PWH (57,58), attributed to complex factors including substances’ effects on PWH’s cognitive ability, which impact their ability to engage in care, as well as concerns about ART and alcohol interactions leading PWH to skip ART when drinking (59). Additionally, substance use may reflect other underlying maladaptive coping strategies (60,61), inaccess to mental health care (62), and other life stresors (63), including sexual violence and unemployment, which collectively make it hard for PWH to stay engaged in HIV care. Therefore, substance use screening at the time of repeat HIV testing may help to predict those at risk for not starting treatment and allow for targeted intervention strategies to counsel on substance use as well as on adaptive coping behaviors to support treatment initiation among RPTs. Studies have shown that individualized and group delivery methods of cognitive behavioral interventions and stress management approaches can be effective across heterogeneous groups of PWH (64–67). Particularly given the heavy counseling burden on HIV lay counselors and providers of HIV testing in South Africa (68), it is important to identify RPTs as PWH who may particularly benefit from targeted counseling and tailor approaches to their needs.

### Limitations and Future Directions

We found no difference in ART initiation between RPTs and first-time positive testers; however, differences may have been masked by the presence of future RPTs among first-time testers. We also found no association between treatment initiation and the other psychosocial factors we assessed, although perceived ART inefficacy (69), symptoms (70), fatalism (71), and clinic barriers (72) have been shown previously to be associated with treatment refusal. Given that these findings did not emerge in this study, we suggest further research to replicate and further explore them. In addition, data on prior testing was by self-report, which is subject to recall bias and may also underestimate the true proportion of RPTs, as it has been shown that around one third of persons thought to be newly diagnosed do not disclose their positive status when testing (3,4). Non-disclosure of a positive status to study staff has also been a concern in recent studies evaluating HIV self-testing among men (73–75). As discussed, this cohort was recruited in the era of CD4 count-based guidelines for treatment eligibility, limiting our ability to generalize these findings in today’s UTT era. However, recent research finding repeat positive testing in South Africa (4,75) suggests that this phenomenon is not limited to the pre-UTT era. A further limitation is that the sample from the main study was limited to people who returned for their CD4 count within six weeks, potentially biasing our results towards individuals relatively more likely to be engaged in the health system than those who did not return for their CD4 count within that time frame. Lastly, our sample sizes of total RPTs and previously ART-eligible RPTs are relatively small, limiting our ability to detect statistically significant differences in these analyses, including the non-significant findings for the other psychosocial factors examined. Qualitative research may help to further elucidate the psychosocial and structural drivers of repeat testing among PWH and the factors influencing their treatment initiation.

## CONCLUSIONS

The prevalence of repeat testing among PWH suggests that testing may overestimate the proportion of newly diagnosed individuals, highlighting the complexity of ways in which PWH engage in HIV care as well as the importance of linkage in order to reach 95–95-95 goals. RPTs may be retesting as a way of managing their diagnosis instead of or prior to starting treatment. In fact, a significant cohort of PWH do not start treatment despite repeat testing, especially those previously eligible for treatment and those using substances. RPT’s engagement in care by virtue of repeat testing offers opportunities to identify these vulnerable PWH and to tailor counseling interventions to address their individualized coping mechanisms and promote treatment initiation.
